name: Carbon dioxide, captured at cement production plant, with heat recovery, for subsequent reuse
generalComment:
Capture of CO2 from a cement plant for subsequent reuse. It is a facility integrated in a synthetic fuel production chain, so a certain amount of the needed steam heat (used to regenerate the sorbent) can come from excess heat generated by the synfuel conversion process, the rest being complemented by a dedicated source. In Meunier et al. 2020, 26% comes from excess heat generated by the methanol production process. To be changed according to needs. Also, there is no need for water, as it is provided by the methanol production process as well. CO2 chemical absorption-regeneration process using amines as scrubbing solvent. The amine solution used for this absorption was an aqueous solution of monoethanolamine (MEA) in a mass concentration of 30 wt.%, widely studied and considered as a benchmark for industrial CO2 capture applications. The CO2 is pre-compressed at 2 bar before storage. 11% of the CO2 is released back into the atmosphere (because the CO2 absoprtion rate is only 90%). The MEA makeup has been considered to 1 kg MEA per ton captured CO2 to compensate the losses due to the thermal degradation of the amine only, as the evaporation of the amine in the absorber is prevented by a flash tank. The rate of fossil vs. biogenic CO2 received from the cement plant need to be reflected in this dataset in two places: at the leakage level, but also at the storage level. At the storage level, we only indicate biogenic CO2. By default, we asusme 6% of the CO2 emissions are biogenic. Here, heat recovery from the cement plant's flue. gases is considered to the extent of 30% of the heat requirement by the capture plant (2.5 GJ/t CO2 captured, instead of 3.66). Source: Alternative production of methanol from industrial CO2. Meunier et al. 2020. Renewable Energy 146, pp. 1192-1203
